"In lighter news" is a phrase used to introduce a story, topic, or piece of information that is fun, cheerful, amusing, or less serious compared to what was just being discussed.

The word "lighter" here is used in the sense of less heavy — not in weight, but in emotional or mental weight. Think of it this way: some news feels heavy (sad, scary, stressful), and some news feels light (happy, funny, uplifting). "In lighter news" is a signal that you are switching from the heavy to the light.

This phrase was born in journalism and broadcasting — specifically in TV and radio news. A typical news broadcast covers serious topics: wars, crimes, economic crises, political scandals, disasters. These stories are important but emotionally draining for the audience.

News anchors and journalists discovered over time that ending a broadcast — or breaking up a long stretch of serious stories — with something warm, funny, or heartwarming helped the audience feel better. So they needed a smooth, verbal signal to make that shift. "In lighter news..." became that signal.

You can think of it as a gear-shift phrase. It tells the listener or reader: "We are done being serious for a moment. Something enjoyable is coming."
Breaking Down the Phrase Word by Word

• "In" — This simply means "on the topic of" or "within the category of." It's the same "in" as in phrases like "in other news" or "in sports today."
  • "Lighter" — This is a comparative adjective. It means less serious, less emotionally heavy, more cheerful. It is the opposite of "heavier," which would mean more grave or distressing.
  • "News" — This refers to any piece of information, story, or update being shared — not necessarily a formal news broadcast. In everyday conversation, people use "news" loosely to mean any new information.

Together: "On the topic of something less serious and more cheerful..."
How and When People Use It

1. In Formal News Broadcasting

A TV news anchor might say:

"Protests continued in the capital today for the third consecutive day. In lighter news, a dog in Ohio has learned to paint portraits of its owners, and one just sold for $3,000."

The phrase acts like a bridge between a serious story and a feel-good one.

2. In Newspapers and Online Articles

Writers use it to transition between sections:

"The city's budget crisis remains unresolved. In lighter news, the local school's science fair produced a student invention that can sort recyclables automatically."

3. In Everyday Conversation

Regular people use it too, not just journalists. If you are chatting with friends and the conversation has been heavy or stressful, you might say:

"Okay, in lighter news — did you hear that they're making a sequel to our favourite movie?"

Here, it works as a polite and smooth way to change the emotional tone of the conversation without being abrupt.
The Tone and Purpose Behind the Phrase

The phrase serves three important functions at once:

  1. It acknowledges the previous topic. By saying "lighter," you implicitly admit that what came before was heavier or more serious. You are not ignoring or dismissing it — you are simply moving on.
  2. It prepares the audience emotionally. It gives people a split-second mental heads-up: "Relax. Something pleasant is coming." This preparation makes the enjoyable story land even better.
  3. It provides balance. In journalism especially, a broadcast or article that is only doom and gloom can leave the audience feeling hopeless. A light story at the end creates emotional balance and leaves people feeling slightly better.

Here are the kinds of topics typically introduced with this phrase:

  • A funny or unusual animal story (e.g., a bear wandering into a coffee shop)
  • A heartwarming human-interest story (e.g., a 90-year-old graduating from university)
  • A quirky record being broken (e.g., the world's largest pizza)
  • A surprising or amusing local event
  • A celebrity doing something funny or kind
  • A scientific discovery that is fascinating rather than alarming
  • A child doing something impressively cute or clever

Basically, anything that makes people smile, laugh, or feel hopeful qualifies.

You may encounter other phrases that work in a very similar way. These are all variations of the same idea:

  • "On a lighter note..." — Perhaps the most common variation. Used identically.
  • "On a brighter note..." — Same function, emphasizing positivity rather than just reduced seriousness.
  • "In more cheerful news..." — More explicitly positive.
  • "Switching gears..." — A more neutral transition, not always implying lighter content.
  • "In other news..." — A general topic shift, not necessarily to something lighter.
  • "And finally..." — Used specifically at the end of a broadcast, often to signal a light closing story.

Among all of these, "in lighter news" and "on a lighter note" are the ones most clearly tied to a shift in emotional tone from heavy to cheerful.

Some people think "lighter" in this phrase refers to less important news. That is not quite right. "Lighter" refers to emotional weight, not significance. A story can be important and still be light — for example, a town celebrating its 200th anniversary is significant to that community but emotionally warm and cheerful. Conversely, a trivial but tragic accident would be emotionally heavy.

The distinction is about how the story makes you feel, not about how newsworthy it is.
A Simple Way to Always Remember It

Here is a memory trick: Imagine you are carrying two bags.

  • One bag is filled with rocks — heavy, tiring, difficult to carry. That is the serious news.
  • The other bag is filled with feathers — easy, airy, pleasant. That is the lighter news.

When someone says "in lighter news," they are putting down the bag of rocks and picking up the bag of feathers — and inviting you to do the same, just for a moment.

"In lighter news" is a transitional phrase that signals a shift from serious, heavy, or distressing content to something more cheerful, fun, or uplifting — used widely in journalism and everyday conversation to provide emotional relief and balance.
